title: Search without AI summaries
summary: Get the ordinary list of links back, with no generated answer on top.
changes: You see the classic list of web results. Nothing about your account changes, and you can go back to normal Google at any time by searching as usual.
how: Google's own "Web" filter — the tab that shows only website links — can be requested directly in the address of the page. ILUD adds that request for you, so the page opens already filtered. It is Google's own feature, not a trick against it.
steps: Search on Google as you normally would.
Under the search box, tap the Web tab. You may need to open the "More" menu to find it.
The generated summary disappears and only website links remain.
caveats: The Web view hides the Images, News, Maps and Videos shortcuts as well. Search again without the filter when you want them.
It applies to that one search. To make it permanent, set it as your default search engine — see the next entry.

title: Make plain results your default
summary: Set your browser so every Google search skips the summary, without thinking about it again.
changes: Every search you type into the address bar goes straight to the plain list of links. Your browsing history, bookmarks and passwords are untouched.

action.label: Copy the search address
action.note: Paste this as a custom search engine in your browser settings. The %s is where your words go.

how: Browsers let you add your own search engine by giving it an address with a placeholder in it. Using Google's Web-filter address as that engine means the filter is applied before the page ever loads.
steps: Desktop Chrome or Edge: Settings → Search engine → Manage search engines → Add. Name it anything, shortcut anything, and paste the address above as the URL. Then set it as default.
Firefox: install the small "add custom search engine" add-on, or use a bookmark keyword with the address above.
Safari on iPhone: Safari cannot take a custom engine. Use the shortcut approach instead — add tenbluelinks.org to your Home Screen, or keep ILUD's search box handy.
Android Chrome: Settings → Search engine → Manage search engines → Add, same as desktop.
caveats: iOS Safari does not allow custom search engines. Third-party browsers on iPhone, such as Chrome or Firefox, do.
Some browser updates reset the default engine. Check it again after a major update.

title: Remove the summary automatically
summary: A small browser add-on strips the generated answer out of every Google page.
changes: Google looks almost exactly as it always did, minus the summary block. Other Google features keep working.
how: These add-ons either hide the summary element on the page, or quietly redirect your search to Google's own Web filter. Both leave the rest of the page intact.
steps: Open your browser's add-on store.
Look for "Hide Google AI Overviews", "Bye Bye Google AI" or "10 Blue Links". All three are widely used and do slightly different jobs.
Install one. There is nothing to configure afterwards.
caveats: Browser add-ons can read the pages you visit. Install ones with a visible author, a public source repository and a large number of users.
Mobile Safari and mobile Chrome do not support these. Firefox for Android does.

title: The blunt one: scare the summary away
summary: Adding one excluded word to a query often stops the summary appearing. It is crude, and it is not dependable.
changes: Your results are the usual ones. One word is excluded from them, which occasionally changes what you find.
how: Google's generated summaries are tied more tightly to its safety filters than its ordinary results are. A query containing a coarse term — even one you have explicitly excluded with a minus sign — can trip those filters, and the summary is simply not produced. The word ILUD appends is Russian profanity; it is there because it reliably trips the filter in English-language searches, not because it means anything useful. Nothing is sent anywhere but Google, and nothing is installed.
steps: Type your search as normal.
Add a space, then a minus sign, then a coarse word — any will do.
Search. The summary is often absent.
caveats: This is a side effect of a filter, not a feature. Google adjusts these filters regularly and the behaviour has come and gone before.
Excluding a word genuinely removes pages containing it, which can quietly change your results.
The Web filter does the same job properly. Use this only when something stops you using that.
Think twice on a shared or work computer where your search history is visible to others.

title: Search somewhere with no AI at all
summary: DuckDuckGo publishes an address that turns off every AI feature it has, permanently, for your browser.
changes: No generated answers, no assistant, no AI images in image search. Ordinary web results, and the same privacy behaviour DuckDuckGo is known for.
how: noai.duckduckgo.com is DuckDuckGo's own address for a version of the engine with every AI feature switched off. Visiting it stores that preference in your browser, so the ordinary address behaves the same way afterwards.
steps: Open noai.duckduckgo.com once in each browser you use.
The setting is stored in that browser. Clearing your site data resets it.
You can also set it feature by feature under Settings → AI Features on duckduckgo.com.
caveats: The preference lives in your browser's storage. Private windows and cleared cookies lose it.
DuckDuckGo's web results come partly from Bing's index, so what you find will differ from Google.

title: Google's results, without Google's summary
summary: Startpage fetches Google's results for you and hands them over as plain links.
changes: The same results you would get from Google, with the summary, the assistant and the tracking stripped out along the way.
how: Startpage acts as a go-between. It runs your search against Google's index on its own servers and returns only the list of links, so the generated layer never reaches you.
caveats: Results can be a little slower than searching Google directly.
Google's own panels — Maps, Flights, Scholar — are not carried across.

title: Search an index nobody else owns
summary: An independent British search engine that crawls the web itself and shows only links.
changes: Different results from Google or Bing, because the index is genuinely separate. No summaries, no chat, no account.
how: Mojeek runs its own crawler and its own index. Very few engines in the world do, which is why its results feel different rather than merely re-skinned.
caveats: A smaller index means fewer results for obscure or very recent queries. Best as a second opinion rather than a sole engine.

title: Find small, hand-written websites
summary: A search engine that deliberately favours personal sites, essays and pages nobody optimised.
changes: You get the sort of page a person wrote because they cared about the subject. Almost nothing commercial surfaces.

action.label: Search the small web
action.placeholder: A subject you want to read about

how: Marginalia ranks pages roughly opposite to the usual way: it prefers plain documents, little advertising, and text that reads as though a human wrote it for another human.
caveats: Not useful for shopping, news, opening hours or anything time-sensitive.
Wonderful for hobbies, history, technical writing and rabbit holes.

title: Browse the old, hand-made web
summary: A small curated index of simple, personal pages of the kind the web used to be made of.
changes: Results are pages people built by hand. There is also a button that simply takes you somewhere at random.
how: Wiby's index is submitted and reviewed by people rather than crawled at scale, so everything in it was chosen by someone.
caveats: Tiny index. Treat it as a place to wander, not a reference tool.

title: Turn off Brave's answer box
summary: Brave Search has a proper switch for its generated answers. Set it once.
changes: Brave Search returns to a plain list of results. Brave's browser assistant is a separate setting.
steps: Open search.brave.com and tap the settings icon.
Find the AI or Answers section.
Switch the answer box off. The preference is stored in your browser.
caveats: The setting is per-browser rather than per-account unless you are signed in.

title: Pay for a search engine that obeys you
summary: A subscription search engine with no advertising, generated answers off by default, and the power to demote sites you dislike.
changes: You pay a monthly fee instead of being the product. You can permanently push chosen domains down, or off your results entirely.
how: Because there is no advertising to protect, Kagi lets you rank the web yourself: block a domain and it never appears again. Its summariser exists but stays off unless you ask for it.
caveats: It costs money. That is the trade, and it is a fair one to state plainly.
There is a free trial with a limited number of searches, so you can judge before paying.

title: Hide AI-written websites from your results
summary: Subscribe to a maintained list of sites known for machine-written filler and they stop appearing in search.
changes: Results from listed domains are removed across Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Brave, Startpage and others.
how: uBlacklist is a browser add-on that removes chosen domains from search result pages. The community blocklist is a long, manually curated register of sites publishing generated text and images. Subscribing means the list keeps itself up to date.
steps: Install the uBlacklist add-on for Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
Open its options and choose "Add a subscription".
Paste the list address from the project page above.
Optionally add the stricter "nuclear" list, which also removes mixed sites that host both human and generated work.
caveats: The list is made by volunteers and will occasionally be wrong in both directions.
The stricter list removes large, legitimate sites such as stock libraries. Start with the ordinary list.
Firefox for Android supports add-ons. Safari and Chrome on iPhone do not.

title: Search only pages written before the flood
summary: Limit results to pages published before generated articles became common.
changes: You see older pages only. Excellent for reference, recipes and how-to writing; useless for anything current.

action.label: Search older pages
action.placeholder: A recipe, a how-to, a definition

how: Google supports a before: operator that limits results by publication date. Combined with the Web filter it gives you a list of older, human-written pages.
caveats: Publication dates on the web are frequently wrong, so the cut is approximate.
Unsuitable for news, prices, opening hours or anything that changes.

title: Go straight to the encyclopedia
summary: For a fact, skip search entirely and read the article people wrote and argued over.
changes: You land on an encyclopedia article with visible authorship, citations and a full edit history.
how: Wikipedia's articles are written and reviewed by people, and every claim is supposed to carry a source you can follow. Generated summaries on the site remain experimental rather than the default for readers.
caveats: Wikipedia has its own biases and gaps. The citations at the foot of an article are the real prize.
Community debate about machine-assisted editing continues; reader-facing article text is still human-written.
